subject: Climate & Environment
title: National Parks and Protected Areas
description: A quick, practical guide to National Parks and Protected Areas.

hook.text: About 17% of the world's land surface is now designated as protected area.

buildup.text: National parks, reserves, and sanctuaries restrict logging, mining, and development.

discovery.text: Protected forests have 50% less deforestation than unprotected ones nearby.

twist.text: But a third of protected areas are 'paper parks' — protected by law, not by enforcement.

climax.text: The global target is to protect 30% of land and ocean by 2030 — the '30 by 30' goal.

punchline.text: A park without rangers is just a line on a map.

quiz.question: What is the '30 by 30' conservation goal?
options: Protect 30% of land and ocean by 2030

details.summary: Protected areas like national parks and wildlife reserves cover roughly 17 percent of global land and are the cornerstone of biodiversity conservation. Their effectiveness varies widely depending on funding, enforcement, boundary design, and community engagement.
details.whyItMatters: Protected areas are the most direct tool for preventing habitat destruction. Their expansion to 30 percent by 2030 is a global policy goal, but quality matters as much as quantity.
takeaways: About 17 percent of global land is in some form of protected status
Roughly a third of protected areas face intense human pressure
Well-funded parks are highly effective at preventing deforestation

faq.question: Are all protected areas effective at stopping deforestation?
faq.answer: No. Many protected areas exist only on paper. A study found that roughly a third face intense human pressure including logging, farming, and infrastructure. Effective protection requires adequate staffing, funding, and community support.

faq.question: How much does it cost to manage protected areas properly?
faq.answer: Estimates suggest effective management of the global protected area network requires 25 to 35 billion dollars per year. Current spending is roughly 10 billion, leaving a persistent gap that undermines conservation outcomes.
